name: Burning and Suppression of Solids – II
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), BASS small flow duct (wind tunnel)
objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow in microgravity, and begin to bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 and real material flammability in microgravity.

fuel.geometry: thin PMMA films, PMMA slabs (one- and two-sided), PMMA rods, PMMA spherical section, fabric strips
fuel.size: films 0.1–0.4 mm thick, slabs 1–5 mm thick, 1–2 cm wide; rods 1/4–1/2 in (6.35–12.7 mm) diameter

varied: ambient O2 concentration (N2 vitiation of the MSG working volume)
constant: pressure ~1 atm (MSG working volume; stated in NASA/TM-20210011385, not measured per test)
diagnostics: video camera with data overlay (fan, flow, radiometer)
resultSummary: About 130 flame tests on PMMA films, slabs, rods, fabrics and a candle in a small wind tunnel on the ISS, with O2 reduced below 21 % by nitrogen dilution. Flames were very sensitive to air flow between 0 and 5 cm/s and could survive at flows below 1 cm/s as dim blue flames that flare up when flow increases. Measured heat-release rates were mostly below 100 W.

keyFindings.text: Flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0–5 cm/s and can be sustained at speeds below 1 cm/s, where they become dim, blue and stable; they can flare up quickly if the air flow suddenly increases.
BASS-II was the first ISS test to dilute the MSG working volume with N2, adding ambient O2 as a controlled variable.
Heat-release rates computed from O2 consumption were well below 100 W for most tests; the global equivalence ratio was fuel-rich (about 1.3 on average).
Hypothesis tested: with adequate ventilation, materials in microgravity burn as well as or better than in normal gravity, so the 1-g upward-burning test may not be conservative for space.

earthRelevance: Validated combustion models apply to wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion (PSI research impacts).

dataNotes: Outcome source: the 'Test observations and anomalies' column of NASA/TM-20210011385 Appendix A (Tables A.1–A.6), extracted with word coordinates by pipeline/extract_tm_bass2.py into data/raw/ntrs/TM-20210011385_appendixA.json; joined on test number for 126 of 129 PSI rows. The 3 rows not in the TM (O20–O22, run in 2016) use the PSI fan/air text (extra.outcomeDerivation = 'keyword-rule').

Outcome semantics: the outcome is what happened at the row's stated (initial) O2 and flow — flame_spread/burned = a flame established and was sustained; self_extinguished = only a brief flame; no_ignition = material did not ignite. Most tests then stepped the flow down to quenching or up to blow-off; that end state is in extra.terminalEvent, not in outcome. Observation text is in extra.tmObservations; 10 cells needing interpretation were read manually (extra.outcomeNote starts with 'manual reading').

spreadRateMmS: Miller PMMA slab tests M1–M20 from TM Table 5.1 (first velocity/rate pair; all pairs in extra.tmTable5_1; M6 and M12 'Not tracked'), and B1 = 2.2 mm/s from TM §2.1.2.1. Other PIs report spread rates only in figures — not digitised.

pressureKpa = 101.3: the TM states 'Ambient pressure was 1 atm' for the T'ien tests and uses P = 1 atm for the MSG work volume in its O2-consumption analysis; the value is not measured per test (basis in extra.pressureSource).
flowCmS = first value of the 'Air display' column (duct flow speed in cm/s per the BASS-II ReadMe); flow was usually stepped during a test and the full sequence is kept in extra['Air display'].
o2Pct = 'Calibrated initial O2 % by vol'. Some 'final O2' values (e.g. 1.6, 0.6, 39.1, 40.4) are clearly sensor artefacts and are kept only in extra.

Rod diameters converted from inches (1/4" = 6.35 mm, 3/8" = 9.525 mm, 1/2" = 12.7 mm). Rows T9 and T18 are dated 2018 in the PSI table (F4, T9, T10, T18 in the TM) although GMT 175 matches 2014 — kept as given in extra.

5 discrepancies between TM-20210011385 and the PSI table: F4: date TM 6/24/2018 vs PSI 6/24/2014; T9: TM Table 7.1 says 'No ignition', Appendix A says 'Brief ignition but flame extinguished before spreading beyond igniter' (kept self_extinguished); T10: date TM 6/24/2018 vs PSI 6/24/2014; T10: TM Table 7.1 says 'No ignition', Appendix A says 'Brief ignition but flame extinguished before spreading beyond igniter' (kept self_extinguished); T12: TM Table 7.1 says 'No ignition', Appendix A says 'Extinguished quickly' (kept self_extinguished).

name: Burning and Suppression of Solids
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), BASS flow duct (76 x 76 mm cross-section) with N2 suppression jet
objective: Bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests and real material flammability in microgravity, and assess how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent (N2, similar to that used on ISS) puts out flames.

fuel.geometry: fabric strips, PMMA spheres and slabs, sheets, candles and wax slabs
fuel.size: 1–2 cm wide fabric strips; 1 and 2 cm PMMA spheres

varied: ambient O2 (some 2013 tests vitiated with N2)
constant: ISS cabin pressure (~0.97–1.0 atm per as-run matrix)
resultSummary: Over a hundred small-scale ISS tests burned fabrics, PMMA spheres and slabs and candles in a low-speed air flow, sometimes followed by an N2 jet to try to extinguish them. Flames were especially sensitive to flow in the 0–5 cm/s range; at the lowest flows they became dim and blue but could keep burning for a long time.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity flames were especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0–5 cm/s, and responded to flow changes with almost no delay.
Even the smallest acrylic-slab flames burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing — a tiny flame could go undetected for a long time and flare up if convection increases.
Using N2 as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned ISS extinguishment techniques.

earthRelevance: Microgravity-validated combustion models feed back into terrestrial fire models (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment (2013)

dataNotes: The PSI experimental table only lists date, test numbers and material. O2, pressure, duct flow and observations are joined from 'PSI-26_Science Documents_As Run_Test Matrix.xlsx' (sheet 'as run matrix') on (As Run Test #, Test #).

Outcome is derived by keyword rules (extra.outcomeDerivation = 'keyword-rule') from the free-text 'Test Observations' column of the As-Run matrix; outcomeRaw keeps the first 240 characters. No better per-test source exists in data/raw: the BASS final report listed on PSI (PSI-26_Reports_BASS_FinalReport.pdf) returns HTTP 404, and NASA/TM-20210011385 covers BASS-II only (its Table 7.1 lists 4 BASS SIBAL tests without outcomes).

Outcome semantics as for BASS-II: the outcome describes the row's initial O2/flow (flame established and sustained -> burned/flame_spread; brief flame only -> self_extinguished; material did not ignite -> no_ignition). How the test ended (flow reduced to quench, flow off, N2 blow-out, burn-out) is in extra.terminalEvent. Igniter failures are 'unknown', not no_ignition.
flowCmS = first value in 'Air display' (cm/s); flow was usually stepped during a test (full sequence in extra.airDisplayCmS). No spread-rate column exists.
O2 fraction (e.g. 0.221) converted to %, pressure converted from atm to kPa (x101.325).

name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment – I
hardware: Saffire-I flow duct in the Cygnus cargo vehicle (after unberthing from ISS)
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's 1-g material screening test.

fuel.geometry: single large fabric sheet in a flow duct

resultSummary: The first intentionally large fire set inside an orbiting spacecraft: a 94 x 40.6 cm cotton-fiberglass sheet burned in a 20 cm/s air flow, once with and once against the flow. In concurrent spread the flame size stayed limited after ignition, unlike the accelerating upward fire seen on Earth.

keyFindings.text: The 94 x 40.6 cm sample was an order of magnitude larger than anything previously burned in microgravity.
In concurrent spread the flame size remained constrained after ignition — qualitatively different from Earth, where an upward-spreading flame on a sample this size accelerates and grows.
The flame in the large Saffire duct spread more slowly than in earlier small-tunnel microgravity tests, attributed to flow acceleration by hot-gas expansion in small tunnels — scale matters.

earthRelevance: Fire behaviour in small sealed volumes informs fire safety in mines, aircraft and submarines (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (2017)
The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) – Objectives, Development and Status (2016)

dataNotes: PSI record dates (2001–2008) appear to be copied from another record and do not match the Cygnus flight; years left null.
Only 2 burn tests (S1 concurrent, S2 opposed); rows F1/F2 (pre-test flow visualisation) are not tests and are skipped.
PSI table header says 'Sample Thickness (cm) = 0.37'. The same SIBAL fabric is listed as 0.37 mm in Saffire-II, so the unit is doubtful; thicknessMm left null (raw value in extra).
PSI table gives length 40.6 cm and width 94 cm; PSI text describes the sample as ~0.94 m long and 0.4 m wide (columns appear swapped).

No spread rate in the PSI table. Outcome 'burned' is based on the reported burn time only.

name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment – II
hardware: Saffire flow duct in the Cygnus pressurized cargo module
objective: Measure low-g flammability of several spacecraft materials at realistic scale and compare with NASA's 1-g material flammability screening test.

fuel.size: 5 cm x 29 cm each, 0.27–10 mm thick

resultSummary: Nine material samples were burned one after another in a Cygnus vehicle. Thin silicone did not sustain a flame in microgravity, while cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full 29 cm length at 2.1–2.6 mm/s. Thick PMMA flames stayed anchored near the base, spreading far more slowly than the 1-g comparison.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity flame spread over SIBAL fabric in 20 cm/s concurrent flow was 2.1–2.6 mm/s, burning the full 29 cm sample (PSI test table).
Silicone samples ignited (80 W, 9.2 s) but had insignificant burn time in microgravity, while in the 1-g comparison the thinnest (0.27 mm) silicone sample burned completely.
Reducing pressure slows concurrent flame spread over thick PMMA toward the microgravity value; a mixed-convection correlation extrapolated to low pressure predicts the Saffire II spread rate.

earthRelevance: Low-pressure ground tests may approximate untested gravity levels for thick and thin solids (NTRS 20200000557).

dataNotes: 9 samples on one card. Microgravity spread rate is given only for the two SIBAL samples (2.1 and 2.6 mm/s); 1-g comparison columns are kept in extra.

Material cells for 2-6 and 2-9 are blank in the PSI CSV (merged cells); filled from the row above and flagged in extra.materialInferred.

name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment – III
hardware: Saffire-III flow duct in the Cygnus cargo vehicle
objective: Repeat the Saffire-I large-scale fabric burn at a higher flow (30 cm/s) to see how rapidly a large fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady spread rate.
resultSummary: Two large SIBAL sheets were burned in a Cygnus vehicle at 30 cm/s air flow (one concurrent, one opposed), extending Saffire-I's 20 cm/s case. The PSI table lists conditions only; no burn results are tabulated.

keyFindings.text: Saffire-III used the same SIBAL material as Saffire-I but a higher flow velocity of 30 cm/s (vs 20 cm/s), with concurrent and opposed flow.
The Saffire series is designed to reduce uncertainty in spacecraft fire-safety design by testing at realistic length scales in an uncrewed vehicle.

earthRelevance: Fire behaviour in sealed vehicles informs fire safety in mines, aircraft and submarines (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) – Objectives, Development and Status (2016)

dataNotes: PSI table has only sample geometry, flow (30 cm/s) and direction: no O2, pressure, burn time, spread rate or outcome -> those fields are null/'unknown'.

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
objective: Map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity, measure the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants (CO2, He) and determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI) as a function of pressure and suppressant concentration.
diagnostics: droplet and flame imaging (droplet diameter history, burning rate, extinction diameter)
resultSummary: 274 droplet tests burned methanol and heptane in mixtures of O2, N2, CO2 and He at 0.7–3 atm. Each test ended in flame extinction, droplet disruption or burning to completion. The data give the oxygen level below which these fuels stop burning and how much CO2 or helium is needed.

keyFindings.text: The limiting oxygen index for methanol droplets in O2–N2–CO2 and O2–N2–He mixtures is around 12–13 % O2 by volume.
Droplets of ~1.5–4 mm captured both diffusive extinction (too little residence time) and radiative extinction (too much heat loss).
FLEX was designed to assess fire suppressants in microgravity and the effect of candidate crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression.

earthRelevance: Suppressant effectiveness results can inform less harmful fire-suppression systems; relevant to submarines and high-altitude aircraft (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: NASA/TP: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (2015)
Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity (2013)
Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus – Flame Extinguishment Experiment (2009)

dataNotes: FLEX test 114 has ambient pressure 0 mmHg in the PSI table (recording error); pressureKpa set to null.
PSI header 'Burning rate; mm' is the droplet burning-rate constant K in mm²/s (values 0.05–1.06; the 0.3–1.06 bulk matches typical d²-law constants); stored as burningRateMm2S.

PSI headers 'O/N/CO/He initial ambient composition' are O2, N2, CO2, He mole fractions (subscripts lost in the CSV). Converted to %; the suppressant (CO2 or He) is reported in diluent/diluentPct, otherwise N2.
Pressure converted from mmHg to kPa (x0.13332). Source file is cp1252-encoded; '–' cells are treated as missing.
flowCmS is null: the table does not state per-test flow; most FLEX tests were quiescent (free or tethered droplets), some had slow drift/translation (not tabulated).
Outcome mapping: Extinction -> extinguished, Disruption -> disruption (droplet disruption/test end), Completion -> completed (burned to completion).
NASA/TP-20150023456 reports 284 tests from Mar 2009–Dec 2011; the PSI table has 274 rows.

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
objective: Extend FLEX to fuels and conditions closer to real combustors: bi-component droplets, soot formation, extinction boundaries, droplet arrays and slow convective flow, to provide benchmark data for numerical models.

fuel.geometry: single droplets and binary droplet arrays, free or fiber-supported

resultSummary: FLEX-2 burned single and paired droplets of pure fuels and mixtures in O2/N2 and O2/He atmospheres at 0.5–3 atm to provide benchmark data for droplet combustion models. PSI publishes only the planned test matrix, not per-test results.

keyFindings.text: Independently varied parameters were fuel type, ambient gas composition, pressure, initial droplet diameter, droplet translation velocity, and droplet spacing in a binary array.

ISS droplet experiments with large bi-component (n-decane/hexanol) droplets at elevated pressure showed a very weak visible hot flame while the burning rate stayed relatively high, suggesting coexisting cool and hot flames.

earthRelevance: Benchmark droplet data support surrogate fuels and cleaner, more efficient combustor and jet-engine design (PSI research impacts).

name: Cool Flames Investigation
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
objective: Study low-temperature 'cool flame' droplet combustion of n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures at 0.5–5 atm, including helium dilution, and relate droplet size, pressure and extinction.
resultSummary: 79 unique droplet tests explored how dodecane droplets keep burning after the visible hot flame goes out, sustained by an invisible low-temperature 'cool flame'. Hot- and cool-flame burning rates and extinction diameters are tabulated for most tests.

keyFindings.text: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet burning was first observed on the ISS; these flames are not visible to the naked eye.
Helium dilution drastically increases the cool-flame extinction diameter compared with N2, CO2 or Xe, while Xe gives longer burning and smaller extinction diameter.

earthRelevance: Cool-flame chemistry matters for ignition of practical fuels and for HCCI / diesel engine design (PSI research impacts).

Some hot-flame k values are very small (0.001–0.2 mm²/s), mostly at 17 % O2 where the hot flame extinguished quickly; values are as given in the DataSummary spreadsheet.

name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), Comparative Soot Diagnostic hardware with aging chamber
objective: Measure the size of smoke particles produced by overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity and relate them to smoke generation and transport, to evaluate and design spacecraft smoke detectors.

fuel.geometry: heated samples in a smoke-generation tube

conditions.assumptionNote: assumption: ISS cabin air (21% O2, 101.3 kPa). The test ran in the MSG work volume on the ISS (SAME Final Science Report p.20-21; SAME-R Final Report p.9: smoke 'diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume'); neither report states O2 or pressure or mentions a purge or backfill gas (N2 was added only to dilute the sampled aerosol). MSG work-volume N2 dilution was first used later, by BASS-II (NTRS 20150019858).

varied: air flow past sample (2–8 cm/s in the flown tests)
smoke aging time (~10 s to ~33 min)
diagnostics: DustTrak aerosol monitor and ionization detector (Commercial Diagnostic Enclosure)
resultSummary: Spacecraft materials were overheated on the ISS to produce smoke, which was aged and measured by detectors and particle samplers. The hypothesis was that low-gravity smoke particles grow larger than on Earth, which could change how smoke detectors respond.

keyFindings.text: Hypothesis: without buoyant flow, smoke particles grow larger in microgravity (longer residence time near the source), which may stop some detectors from alarming.
All current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed from normal-gravity data; earlier shuttle experiments saw larger particles in low gravity in some cases.
After SAME, the TEM grids returned to the ground were contaminated with foreign particles and unusable, which motivated the SAME-R reflight.

earthRelevance: Better smoke detectors for extreme environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories (PSI research impacts).

name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment – Reflight
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), SAME hardware with M-pass instrument
objective: Repeat SAME with new materials (Pyrell foam), wider conditions (higher heating, no-flow heating) and better diagnostics to quantify smoke particle size distributions in low gravity.

resultSummary: SAME-R completed 66 test points on the ISS in July–September 2010 with five spacecraft materials. Most average smoke particle sizes were 200–400 nm, with some quiescent (no-flow) cases producing substantially larger particles.

keyFindings.text: The majority of average smoke particle sizes were in the 200–400 nm range, with quiescent cases producing some substantially larger particles.
Smoke was aged for 11 to 1800 s to simulate transport time from source to detector; flow past the sample ranged from quiescent to 8 cm/s.
SAME-R flight tests ran from July 16 to September 9, 2010, completing 66 test points.

earthRelevance: Detector designs from SAME data apply to submarines and underwater laboratories (PSI research impacts).

name: ACME – Burning Rate Emulator
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME modular hardware, porous flat burner with heat-flux gauge
objective: Use a gas burner that emulates condensed (solid/liquid) fuels to find the conditions for steady burning in a quiescent microgravity ambient, including candidate spacecraft atmospheres (21 % O2 at 14.7 psia, 26.5 % at 10.2 psia, 34 % at 8.2 psia).
diagnostics: heat-flux gauge and burner surface temperature
resultSummary: A gas-fed burner emulating solids like PMMA and nylon burned in still air on the ISS. In elevated-oxygen atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft the flames kept burning without any air flow, whereas at 21 % O2 they self-extinguished in a short time.

keyFindings.text: Quasi-steady burning of emulated condensed materials (e.g. PMMA, nylon) was observed in microgravity without air flow — even though stopping ventilation is a standard step in fighting spacecraft fires.
Sustained burning without air flow was seen in elevated-O2 atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas flames at 21 % O2 self-extinguished quickly.
Results suggest NASA may want to increase use of its cone-calorimeter Test 2, which can measure the material properties that govern these microgravity flames.

earthRelevance: Links microgravity flammability to cone-calorimeter (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2) material properties (PSI research impacts).

name: ACME – Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME modular hardware, spherical porous burner
objective: Determine the conditions for steady cool diffusion flames of gaseous fuels on spherical porous burners, for normal and inverse flames over a broad range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature and flow rate.

fuel.geometry: spherical porous burner (normal: fuel out; inverse: oxidizer out)

resultSummary: Spherical gas flames on the ISS were used to look for cool flames and to map when flames ignite, self-extinguish or burn until the fuel is cut. Inverse flames reached the highest oxygen levels flown in these data (oxidizer stream up to 85 % O2), but they are gas flames, not burning materials.

keyFindings.text: Hypotheses include demonstrating, for the first time, steady cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners, inverse cool diffusion flames, and cool flames over a wide range of Zst, Tad and pressure.
ACME's six investigations of gaseous non-premixed flames ran on the ISS from Nov 2017 to Feb 2022; three of them used porous spherical burners giving a nominally one-dimensional flame.

earthRelevance: Cool-flame kinetics could enable ultra-lean, higher-efficiency engines (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: ACME: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (poster, 2022)
Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station (2021)

dataNotes: Two PSI tables: normal flames (179 rows) and inverse flames (154 rows; the CSV has ~860 trailing blank lines which are skipped).
For inverse flames o2Pct is the O2 fraction of the oxidizer stream leaving the burner (up to 85 %), not an ambient atmosphere — do not compare directly with solid-material tests.

Outcome mapping: Hot ignition 'No' -> no_ignition; 'flash' -> self_extinguished; 'Yes' + SE (self-extinguished) -> self_extinguished; 'Yes' + FT (flow terminated while burning) -> burned. Cool-flame observations are in extra['Cool flame?'].

Pressure 'approx p (bar)' converted to kPa (x100). flowCmS = 0 (spherical burner in a quiescent chamber; fuel/oxidizer mass flow rates are in extra). Diluent assumed N2 per the 'O2/N2' description in PSI text.

name: ACME – Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME coflow and gas-jet burners with high-voltage mesh electrode (up to 10 kV)
objective: Understand how electric fields act on laminar diffusion flames in microgravity: voltage vs chemi-ion current, dynamic flame response, soot formation and stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
diagnostics: filtered spectral imaging (chemiluminescence, soot volume fraction)
resultSummary: Methane and ethylene flames on the ISS were exposed to electric fields of either polarity to study ion-driven flows, soot and flame stability without buoyancy. It is a fundamental combustion study, not a fire-safety test.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity isolates electric-field (ion-driven convection) effects from buoyancy; voltage–current curves reveal ion-driven convection effects.
Electric-field control of flames may reduce pollutant and soot emissions in terrestrial combustion; the work is not aimed at a space application.

earthRelevance: Electric-field flame control may lower soot and pollutant emissions and improve combustion efficiency (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: Chien et al., Electric-field effects on methane coflow flames aboard the ISS: ACME E-FIELD flames, Combust. Flame 2022
ACME: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (poster, 2022)

dataNotes: Partial gravity: the concept treats E-FIELD as an electric-field analogue of buoyancy; PSI text only states that microgravity isolates field effects from buoyancy.
PSI table is a per-test-day summary (fuel, dilution, electrode polarity, number of flames ignited); rows here are (day x fuel concentration), not individual tests.
Oxidizer O2, pressure, coflow velocity and applied voltage are not in the PSI table -> null. Electric field is applied up to 10 kV (PSI approach text).

name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), SPICE flow duct with nozzles
objective: Find the laminar smoke point (onset of soot emission) of non-buoyant gas-jet flames in co-flowing air and how burner diameter, co-flow velocity and fuel affect it.

fuel.geometry: round jet nozzles in co-flowing air

constant: cabin air co-flow (nominal 21 % O2, 101 kPa per SPICE Final Report)
diagnostics: still and video cameras (flame length, smoke point)
resultSummary: 526 small gas-jet flames were studied in the glovebox to find when they begin to emit soot. Soot governs flame heat emission, so the data help predict fire spread and support material flammability criteria.

keyFindings.text: Soot dominates heat emitted from flames in both normal gravity and microgravity fires; controlling it matters for preventing fire spread.
In total 526 flames were studied, with co-flow velocities from 5.4 to 65 cm/s and three burner diameters.

earthRelevance: Better soot control for jet engines and power-generation boilers (NTRS 20090014827).
dataNotes: The PSI table gives GMT day-of-year only, without the year; years left null.
Each row is one fuel-flow/air-flow setting of an ignited jet flame (several rows share one ignition). flowCmS = co-flow air velocity; nozzle inner diameter in diameterMm.
8 rows have a negative air rate (sensor offset at fan-off); flowCmS set to null, raw value in extra.airRateRaw.

Joined 462 of 469 PSI rows to the master sheet 'PSI-107_Raw Data_Spice Flight Test Data II modified.xls' (sheet 'Data record of Video and Stills', the source of the PSI table) on day, nozzle, fuel rate and air rate in table order. From it: extra.flameLengthMm (luminous flame length from video, mm), extra.nikonFlameHeightMm, extra.smokeHeightFlag ('Smoke Height' Y/N column), extra.flagSH / extra.flagLO (columns headed 'SH ?' / 'LO ?', undocumented — LO is probably lift-off), extra.comment.

smokePointLengthMm = luminous flame length at the smoke point (mm) from the curated sheet 'Smoke Point Datasheet' of 'PSI-107_Raw Data_SmokePointReview-0g-3.xlsx' (55 ISS smoke points; the SPICE Final Report Table 1 counts 52). Attached to 53 PSI rows: same day, nozzle and ignition time, then the fuel/air setting nearest to the review sheet's (the review recomputed fuel rates with corrected meter factors; its values are kept in extra.smokePointAirCmS / smokePointFuelRateSccm); no PSI row with that ignition time for E16-1, 75P16-3. All other rows are not at their smoke point -> null.

o2Pct = 21 and pressureKpa = 101 are the nominal conditions stated in the SPICE Final Report (Table 1 note: '298 K, 101 kPa and 21±1% O2'; coflow is MSG cabin air). The master sheet's 'Pressure (Pa)' column is a constant 101325 (kept in extra.pressurePa). Not measured per test.

Outcome: 'not_applicable' for every row. SPICE deliberately ignited every flame, so 'burned' would be a by-design constant, not a flammability result; SPICE rows are therefore excluded from burn/no-burn estimates and backtests (blow-off comments are kept in outcomeRaw). SPICE's natural per-row result is the smoke point (sooting vs non-sooting); the Final Report notes 'All smoke point flames were attached to the burner, i.e., not lifted'.

name: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), SPICE/SLICE fan-driven flow duct with exchangeable burner tubes
objective: Understand the structure and stability (lift-off, blow-out) of laminar co-flow diffusion flames in microgravity, including fuel dilution effects on soot.
diagnostics: high-resolution color still camera with sensor overlay
soot temperature / volume fraction from flame emission
resultSummary: On 12 test days in 2012, methane, ethylene and other gas flames were photographed in co-flowing air to study lift-off, blow-out and soot. Microgravity flames were longer and sootier than their 1-g counterparts.

keyFindings.text: Microgravity sooting CH4 flames had lower soot temperatures and higher soot volume fractions than normal-gravity flames, with soot shifting from the centerline to the wings.
Non-buoyant luminous flame lengths are proportional to fuel mass flow rate and noticeably longer than 1-g flames; buoyancy narrows the flame by radially inward convection.

earthRelevance: Improved soot and flame-stability models for cleaner engines and industrial burners (PSI research impacts).

sources.label: An Experimental and Computational Study on Soot Formation in a Coflow Jet Flame Under Microgravity and Normal Gravity (2014)
A Computational and Experimental Study of Coflow Laminar Methane/Air Diffusion Flames (2014)
